component.name: ATO20
component.summary: Tabletop RPG scenes on your TV

description.p: ATO20 runs the visual side of a tabletop RPG session played around a real table. You build the next scene on your laptop while the table keeps watching the current one on the TV, and each player follows their own character sheet on their phone.

A campaign is a folder on your disk, like a vault in Obsidian. Maps, portraits, handouts, notes and audio live in it as ordinary files, so you can back it up, sync it or move it to another machine without exporting anything.

Scenes hold maps with tokens, hidden areas, saved camera framings and measuring tools. Boards are scenes without a floor, for planning: free text, arrows that stay anchored to what you move, sticky notes and live Markdown cards. What the table sees is whatever you choose to put on air.
Everything runs on your own machine. The phones and the TV reach it over the local network, so a session works with no internet connection and without an account.

description.p: ATO20 1.1 brings a side-on 2.5D map view in beta, folders and search to Maps, Backgrounds, Characters and Portraits, cropping for portraits and miniatures, opening a sheet with a double click, and image meters for plugins. Fixes close the list.

ul.li: Side-on map view (2.5D), in beta: the table seen at an angle, with the walls standing up. In the GM window, the 2.5D button next to the map settings shows the table side-on: characters stand and walls rise. For the spectator window to see it that way, create a tripod in the Tripods bar and broadcast it with T. In 2.5D you can select, drag and lay characters down; the map, lights and walls are still edited in 2D. Shift+L steps into the tripod and moves it like in a game.

Maps, Backgrounds, Characters and Portraits have folders and search. Drag a map or a character into a folder, or use "Move to" in the row menu. Players and NPCs each have their own tree, and loose portraits show up under the character's folder. Search finds by name and by folder, and shows the path of each result. The Library also has search.

Crop the portrait and the miniature when attaching them, as a square or a circle. Drag to frame and use the wheel to zoom in, up to 8x. The miniature opens as a circle, the round token of the table. "Use whole image" keeps the image as it came, for a full-body figure.
Double-clicking a character on the map opens their sheet. It also works on a locked token, and the token stays in place.

Plugins can draw meters with images: a bar, dots or a sequence of frames, with the value written inside, using only images and a configuration file in the plugin folder. In the meter, the palette puts the built-in shapes and the plugin ones together, and the name and the value can be shown or hidden.
Fixed: with the Table tab open, the table stopped following the GM. The spectator window, the phone and the tab itself froze on a frame from minutes before, with no warning.
Fixed: with many cameras, the camera bar ran across the screen. It now stops growing and scrolls, with faded edges when a camera is out of view.

description.p: ATO20 1.0 brings a campaign chat, map pings, cameras of any shape, an eye in the Layers list and per-item shadows, plus a richer note editor and many smaller changes. Fixes close the list.

ul.li: The campaign has a chat, with the dice rolls inside the conversation. It is stored in the campaign itself and travels with it when exported. On the phone, Chat is a new tab with an "Only to the GM" option; you write to the table, to one player or only to yourself, and can delete any line. @ mentions a character. Your own rolls are visible only to you until you turn on Open dice. The Chat window opens by itself when a player writes, and the Rolls window stays as it was.

Pings: anyone at the table points at a spot on the map, and everybody sees it. On the phone, hold a finger still on the map; on your screen, hold the right button, while a short click still opens the menu. The ' (apostrophe) key opens the wheel on both screens, for touchpad users. There are six: Look here, Careful, Danger, Attack, What is this? and On my way. In the scene on air, the ping shows on your screen, on the TV and on the phones.

A camera can take any shape: the tower standing up, the corridor lying down. Drag a corner of the frame and width and height change independently; with Shift, the shape is kept. The TV shows the whole crop with black bars around it, and portraits stay in the corner of the screen, over the bar. Moving, zooming, following a token or holding V keep the shape, and "Back to 16:9", in the frame's right-click menu, restores the 16:9 around the camera.

The eye in the Layers list takes an image or a folder out of the scene. It disappears from your stage and from the table, as in Figma, and a second click brings it back: the roof in the way while you build the floor below, or the monster waiting for its moment. Hidden items stay out of area selection and Ctrl+A. The row is dimmed in the list, which is where you bring it back from. A folder takes everything inside it, and a hidden token takes its portrait off the table too.

Each image and token chooses how it casts a shadow, from a new shadow button on the gizmo. "At the base" is for a standing figure: a yellow line marks where it stands, and the shadow starts there. "Whole" is for things seen from above, like a round token, a barrel or a treetop: the whole figure stretches away from the light without coming loose, and a slider sets the height. "None" turns it off. It works under the sun and under a torch, and a token flipped vertically no longer casts its shadow from its head.

A note shows what it mentions: the image, the portrait, the map or the book page. Just leave the mention alone on its line. Several on one line sit side by side, and images get a width handle and alignment buttons. The new ! sign points to a bookmarked page on the bookshelf, by the bookmark's name, and its chip opens the book at that page, in notes and sticky notes. In sticky notes and cards, clicking a mention now opens what it points to.

The note editor gained a formatting bar, Ctrl+F and multi-line selection. The bar writes the Markdown for you, as do Ctrl+B and Ctrl+I. Tab indents the line and nests list items. Clicking puts the cursor where you clicked, and dragging or using Shift selects several lines to delete, paste or format. The Mentions panel lists who and what the note mentions, and Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- change the text size. In the Files tab, search now also finds text inside notes, sticky notes and boards.

Sticky notes are written in handwriting, a pen-like font, on your screen and on the TV. With a sticky note or a card selected, Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- step the text size up and down, and the TV now respects that size; with nothing selected, the keys still zoom. The new font is wider, so an old, tightly sized sticky note may hide its last line.

Shapes and arrows can have rounded corners and a hand-drawn stroke, wobbly like a pencil sketch, with loose text in the sticky-note font. Both switches live in the new Board topic of the campaign settings and apply to what is drawn from then on; what is already drawn does not change. On the gizmo, Colour and fill became Style, which changes one shape's stroke and fill colour and opacity, its thickness, corners and hand-drawn stroke.

The gizmo gained a padlock, and walls, hidden areas, shapes, text and lights can now be locked. Before, only images and tokens could, from the Layers list and the menu. Locked, nothing moves by dragging or with the arrow keys, the handles go away and nothing is deleted by accident: the wall no longer comes along when you grab the token beside it, and the boss stays on the altar. Lights can also be locked from the Locked row in their panel.

Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V work on walls, hidden areas, lights, sticky notes and pencil strokes, along with cut and duplicate, and copies keep their colour. Copying is complete now: text keeps its colour, background and bold, polygons keep their vertices, and text and shapes paste on maps too. On a board, pasting a copied shape used to bring in whatever text had been copied outside the app instead.

The campaign settings gained topics and search. Board, Meters, Conditions and the two portrait topics sit on a bar, one open at a time, which becomes a row along the top when the window is narrow in the dock. Search ignores accents and also finds what you created, such as the name of one of your conditions. Plugin adjustments that apply only to this campaign get an Adjustments topic.

Plugins can take the table to another browser, like OBS for a live stream. A plugin serves pages on the network with rolling dice and portraits drawn as on the TV, on a transparent background, and only receives what the table sees. Its code still runs only on your computer. Plugins can also read and post to the campaign chat.

Shift locks the camera to one axis, and a held arrow key moves it smoothly. With Shift, while dragging the frame or holding V, the camera moves only sideways or only up and down, to follow a wall or a corridor. A held arrow used to take a step, stop for half a second and carry on in jumps; it now starts at once and eases to a stop, at a steady speed, a little slower than before and faster with Shift. A tap still moves 5%. Along the way, the wheel with Shift zooms the camera in instead of only out, and V with Shift no longer flips the selection.

A prepared camera is yellow, no longer red. In a scene that is off air, the camera the table will open on showed red, as if the TV were already showing it. Red now belongs only to the camera on air, and a prepared one offers "Undo preparation" instead of "Take off air".

A camera can be removed with the X on its chip, and the frame gained a right-click menu with Remove, Broadcast, Bring to where I am and Go to camera, also on the other cameras drawn on the map. The three-dot menu of the camera bar removes it too. Before, a camera only went away from the chip's right-click menu, and nothing there said so.

Putting a scene on air from the Scenes list also opens it for you: what just went to the TV is what you need at hand. If it was already open, the selection and the zoom stay as they were. To prepare the next scene while the table watches the current one, open it without broadcasting.

A pin's note accepts dragged images, and Delete removes the pin. Attachments became a grid that takes images from the Library and files from your computer. A thumbnail opens in a window on click and goes onto the map by dragging, without leaving the pin. Clicking a pin now drops the previous selection: before, with a token selected, clicking a pin and pressing Delete deleted the token.

Closing the window with a campaign open asks first. Closing drops the TV and the phones in the middle of the session, and the X sits next to maximise. Switching campaigns and removing a campaign from the list on the start screen also ask first. Alt+F4 still closes right away.

Fixed: the TV slides smoothly again when the camera moves. Since 0.2.0, dragging the frame, moving with the arrow keys or holding V reached the table in jumps, ten per second, and only zoom was smooth.

Fixed: walls no longer trap the tokens under them. A wall drawn over a building swallowed the clicks of every token inside it. Tokens now get the click first, and the wall is picked by clicking empty space inside it. At rest it is drawn fainter, so it does not hide the map. Walls and lights dragged off the map also stay visible, so there is something to click to bring them back.

Fixed: dragging a card on a board full of notes no longer stutters. With thirty cards, dragging nearly stalled; it is now smooth. Dragging a token with the scene on air got lighter too. A card's scrollbar only shows with the mouse over it.

Fixed: the gizmo, light and pin note panels no longer go off screen. Near the edge, a panel opens on the other side or tucks inside. A pin's note stays where you dragged it and stops at the edge instead of getting lost beyond it.

Fixed: clicking the map takes the cursor out of a text field, and shortcuts work again. With the character search focused, whatever you typed after clicking the map went into it. Same with sliders: the arrow keys push the selection again.
Fixed: a condition's icon on a token no longer turns into a blot at high zoom.

description.p: Creating a camera with the N key no longer changes what the table is watching. The new camera used to go live at once and cut the table's scene. It is now only selected, the table stays on the camera it was on, and T puts the new one live when it is time. The + button on the camera pill still creates it live.

A camera created with the N key is placed where the mouse is pointing, with the size of the selected camera. With the mouse off the map, over a column or a window on top, it is placed where it used to be.

The map turned black in the viewer window after undoing a background change. Changing or removing a background deletes the old map from the campaign, and Ctrl+Z pointed the scene back at it. The screen kept showing the cached image, and the viewer window went black later. Ctrl+Z no longer touches the background: to go back to the previous map, change it again from the scene menu.

The section of a disabled plugin stayed on the player's phone, with a button that no longer did anything. It now goes away when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, and comes back with what was stored if the plugin returns.
The map grid can now be hexagonal, pointy or flat, set in the grid settings. Snapping puts the token at the centre of the cell, and the cell under the token lights up.

Settings gained an Adjustments section with search and a JSON editor: everything ATO20 and the plugins let you tweak, in one list, per machine and per campaign (the campaign wins). Zoom, the update notice and the volumes moved into that file.

Plugins can change the interface: items in the right-click menus of the token, the light, the hidden area and the lists; new sections on the character sheet; replacing the body of a section or a whole window with their own (disabling the plugin brings the stock one back); and plugin tools with an icon, an options pill and a drag preview.

Plugins reach meters, conditions and dice: read the whole cast, adjust meters in a batch, toggle a condition on the horde, roll real dice on the stage and get notified when something changes. Each plugin stores its own data per character, with a part only the GM sees. Initiative, attack buttons and abilities can now exist as plugins.

A meter can wear the plugin's drawing, on the TV and on the phone: a heart that empties, a bar that pulses, as an SVG with variables. No plugin code runs outside your computer; a TV without the plugin shows the usual bar.

A plugin can put a section with buttons on the player's phone. Tapping sends the action to the GM and the plugin decides what it does; the result shows up on the table. The player's sheet now refreshes by itself when the GM changes it.

Fixes: a broken plugin no longer takes down the GM's screen (the error shows inside its panel); choosing a plugin tool works without opening one of its panels first; a board no longer leaks plugin data to the table; sticky notes and cards accept the right click.

Characters gained conditions: poisoned, prone, blessed — a badge with a name, an icon and a colour, on the sheet right below the meters. The campaign keeps a menu of them, and "Use suggestions" creates eight ready ones. A hidden condition never leaves your computer.

A condition changes the figure: an aura, a tint, translucency, a tremble or a fade, on the token and on the portrait. Badges show above the token, at the top of the portrait and on the owner's phone, and they can be dragged in the portrait layout like the other pieces. The right-click Conditions submenu applies to the whole selection, so a horde can be poisoned at once.

A token's lantern can become a beam that turns with the figure: aim it once where the drawing faces, and rotating the token rotates the beam. The token's right-click menu is down to half its lines, with what belongs to the scene — paste, select all, camera — moved to a right-click on empty space.

Maps can go dark, and the dark has a tone: pitch, night, cave, abyss or a colour of your own. The table sees the full darkness; you see it dimmer, so you can work inside it. The Light tool brings the torch back: one click pins a light with six ready moods — flame, candle, moon, magic, poison, blood —, a free colour, an intensity and two reaches: where the map can be read, and how far a shape can still be made out. Tokens can carry a lantern from the right-click menu, and it walks with the character on the TV and the phones too.

Walls block the light, and each token casts a silhouette away from every flame and turns lighter on the side facing it: three torches in a room give each goblin three shadows. Lights switch off and on while keeping their colour and reach, can become a cone aimed and opened by its handles, and can flicker like fire, pulse or blink — lanterns included. If your system asks for reduced motion, lights hold still.

Moving images now move on the TV and the phones as well: GIF, animated WebP and APNG reach the table whole, including those already in the campaign. In the lists, a play badge marks what is animated, and hovering plays it.

Characters gained meters: a number up to a ceiling, with a name, a colour and a shape — bar, pips or percentage — for hit points, sanity, ammunition, load or a torch. Only the game master writes them, from the sheet, where the bar can be dragged to change the value. The table and the character's owner read them, and a hidden meter never leaves your computer.

At the table, meters sit in a column next to the portrait, and a switch in the map settings puts names and meters above the tokens for combat maps. The campaign gained its own settings window, holding the default meters every character starts with and the layout and position of the portraits. Portraits can also show the character's name; it starts switched off, so no one is introduced before their time.
Fix: opening a campaign no longer blanks the portraits on the TV and the phones for a few seconds.

Maps gained a sun and walls. The sun lights nothing: it only says where shadows fall, and you aim it on a sky seen from above, in the map settings. Walls have a height, so a garden wall and a watchtower cast different shadows, and each token's shadow is its own silhouette — staff, cloak and mount included. The table sees the shadows, never the walls that cast them.

Players can move and rotate their own character's token from the phone: a finger in the middle carries it, a finger on the outer ring turns it. The grid became a map setting with snapping, so tokens land in the middle of a square for the game master and the player alike; hold Alt to drop one exactly where it was released. The square a character stands on lights up on all three screens.

Besides maps, a campaign now has backdrops: the image of a setting with a few figures on top, without camera, grid, fog or sun. The panel is now called Scenes, with a tab for each. A campaign can also have a cover, which is what the TV shows when nothing is on air. Map tools sit exposed on the right edge, the ruler lets go after measuring, and hidden areas moved to a button on the stage.

Fixes: creating or deleting a scene no longer wipes the folders and notes in Files. Right-clicking a token now shows the token's own actions. The TV and the phones follow the sound desk's category faders. Portraits stay still on the TV and phones while the camera moves, and a character whose player left the table loses the blue player outline.

The sound panel became a mixing desk. Several sounds now play at once — rain underneath, a tavern on top, thunder fired on cue — each with its own fader. The numeric keypad turns into pads, so a sound starts with a keystroke instead of a hunt across the screen. Sounds declare whether they are ambience or one-shots, carry their own name and colour, can be searched, and a macro lights a whole set at once. Switching ambience fades instead of cutting, and a scene remembers which ambience it lights.

Drawing now works on the map, not only on the board: shapes, curving arrows and free text, with the tool rail on the edge, and you choose what the table sees. Hidden areas can be square, round or drawn by hand, they rotate, and their vertices stay editable. Character tokens gained an outline that says whose they are.

A character can have several appearances — Wounded, Wolf, Hooded — each holding its own portrait and token image. Switching swaps both at once, including tokens already placed on every map, and can be done from the sheet, the character list or the token itself. Ctrl+V now brings an image in from outside: a screenshot, an editor crop or a picture copied from the browser, landing on the map, on the board or in the library.

Portraits can travel as a group, with a coloured frame, a name, their own order and a corner of the screen. PDF character sheets open in the application's own reader instead of an embedded browser window, and player inventory items gained a photo frame. Creating a character asks for the name first, F2 renames, and renaming behaves the same everywhere: clicking away saves, Enter saves, Escape discards. Empty panels now explain what to do, tabs close with the X or the middle mouse button, and Ctrl+Z no longer deletes scenes, boards or notes.

Fixes: the map no longer jumps and shimmers when zooming, and the handles stop blurring and swelling as the map moves away; the wheel behaves like a real mouse and dragging answers frame by frame. Sound one-shots play the whole file and the ambience relights without blinking, the library bin can see sounds that are not playing, and closing a window that sits behind another no longer takes two clicks.
On Windows, the installer file now shows the ATO20 icon too. Version 0.1.3 fixed the installed app and its shortcut, but the downloaded setup.exe still showed the packaging tool's generic globe.
Packages now ship the ATO20 icon: the tent with a d20 on a dark tile. Until now every build carried the packaging toolkit's default icon.
Fixes the store page announcing the previous version's changes. Behind the scenes only: nothing changes for people running the AppImage or the Windows installer.

Groundwork for the Linux stores. Nothing changes in the app itself: fonts are no longer downloaded while packaging, and the update notice steps aside in store builds, where the store is what updates you.

First beta. Campaigns gain boards: a floorless sheet with free text, anchored arrows and live Markdown cards. Files, notes and images now share one folder tree, dice can be rolled by notation, the ruler became a measuring shape placed on the map, and the bookshelf shows covers.
